article.overview: An autonomous robotic experiment is a payload or test system in which robots carry out in-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) tasks, such as excavating, collecting and moving lunar regolith, with substantial onboard autonomy rather than continuous remote control. The most developed example in the sources reviewed is NASA's ISRU Pilot Excavator (IPEx), a robotic excavator designed to excavate up to 10,000 kg of lunar regolith in a single lunar day [1][3]. NASA design documentation describes IPEx at Technology Readiness Level 5, and its autonomy has been tested in an enclosed terrestrial lunar-analogue facility [2][4]. No flight or lunar operation of IPEx has been verified in the sources reviewed.
article.description: In this catalogue category, an autonomous robotic experiment combines three elements: a mobile or manipulator robot, a task that contributes to ISRU (for example excavation, regolith transport, site preparation or resource prospecting), and autonomy that allows the robot to navigate, detect hazards and make digging decisions without a human operator controlling each movement. The catalogue entry is a generic class. No single design, mass, power or operating mode applies to all such experiments. Lunar conditions make autonomy difficult. NASA notes that low-angle sunlight, long shadows and featureless terrain make navigation difficult, and the IPEx test-site paper reports that low sun angles and long shadows at the lunar south pole make vision-based autonomy difficult [1][4]. Robotic excavation is a precursor to ISRU processing. NASA describes IPEx as supporting ISRU, including extracting oxygen from regolith, by supplying regolith to downstream processing [1].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of an autonomous robotic ISRU experiment is to show that robots can perform the mining and materials-handling steps that ISRU requires without continuous human teleoperation. NASA project material states that IPEx reduces reliance on Earth-supplied resources [1]. Such experiments also test whether autonomy works under the lighting, terrain and dust conditions of the lunar surface. Results inform ISRU system design, operations planning and risk reduction. Broader applications such as site preparation for infrastructure are not demonstrated in the sources reviewed.
article.operating_principle: Excavation in low gravity is difficult because digging forces can push a light machine backwards. The IPEx design, as described by its developers, uses two paired bucket drums that dig simultaneously in opposing directions, so that the reaction forces largely offset one another. This allows a light machine to dig without depending on heavy mass for traction [2][3]. The design also includes a cameras and dust-mitigation subsystem and a thermal control subsystem with an actuated radiator cover and phase-change material [2]. Autonomous operation relies on navigation and excavation algorithms that are still under test, and NASA states that autonomy testing is ongoing [1][4]. Avionics and software are described in a separate publication that was not reviewed for this article [2].
article.scientific_importance: The main value of an autonomous robotic experiment is engineering and operational knowledge rather than new geological measurement. Such experiments test whether robots can dig, transport and navigate reliably in lunar conditions without continuous human control, and how lighting, dust and terrain affect that autonomy. This knowledge is needed before ISRU pilot plants and eventual production systems can be scaled. The IPEx autonomy test-site paper notes that low sun angles and long shadows at the lunar south pole make vision-based autonomy difficult, which is why terrestrial testing in simulated conditions is important before flight [4].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for autonomous robotic experiments. The values below relate to named designs, laboratory test articles or test facilities. Where a value is a NASA goal, a laboratory drum size or a facility dimension, it is labelled as such and must not be read as a measured flight specification. Published mass, dimensions and power for the flight-design IPEx were not found in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: ISRU Pilot Excavator (IPEx)
examples.type: Proposed robotic excavator; Technology Readiness Level 5 design; not flown
examples.mass_class: 30 kg-class robotic excavator, as described in NASA technical material [3]. This is a mass class, not a published measured total mass.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.excavation_goal_note: NASA design goal of excavating up to 10,000 kg of regolith in a single lunar day [1]. This is a target, not a measured rate.
examples.bucket_drums: Paired counter-rotating bucket drums that dig simultaneously in opposing directions [2][3].
examples.lab_bucket_drum_scaling_note: Laboratory test drums used for bucket-drum scaling experiments at Kennedy Space Center, not IPEx flight drums [3]. The source gives diameter and width; drum length is not given.
examples.naming_note: The NASA web page calls the machine the 'Infrastructure Pilot Excavator', while technical papers use 'ISRU Pilot Excavator' [1][2].
examples.qualification: Ground testing in a large Black Point 1 (BP-1) lunar regolith simulant bin at Kennedy Space Center [3]. No flight or lunar operation verified.

examples.name: IPEx Autonomy Test-Site
examples.type: Terrestrial test facility for autonomous excavation (not a flight payload)
examples.dimensions: Enclosed area of 21.3 x 33.5 m for testing excavation technologies under simulated lunar south-pole conditions [4].
examples.power_note: Power draw of the facility lighting is not stated in the sources reviewed.
test_features: High-power lights replicating low solar angles
Motion-capture system providing ground-truth robot poses
examples.qualification: The authors report that the site has been used to evaluate autonomous navigation and excavation, with early results and comparisons against a digital simulation [4].

examples.name: ARISE (Autonomous Robots for In-situ Surface Exploration)
examples.type: Proposed and simulated robot-team concept; project period 01.03.2023 to 29.02.2024 [5]
examples.dimensions: Not specified on the project page.
examples.robots: Legged (walking) and wheeled robots, possibly carrying a top-mounted arm and payloads such as a UV-VIS-NIR microscope, a context imager and spectrometers, according to the project page [5].
examples.operating_concept: A single operator controlling a scalable robot team, with autonomy adjustable from autonomy-assisted teleoperation to intermediate control schemes [5].
examples.qualification: The project page describes a simulated lunar prospecting mission. It does not describe flight, lunar operation or results [5].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for this payload class. The IPEx flight-design dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The laboratory bucket-drum scaling test drums range from 239 mm to 432 mm in diameter [3], and the IPEx test-site facility encloses a 21.3 x 33.5 m area [4]. These are not comparable to one another, and none describes the dimensions of a lander-deliverable flight robot.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: NASA technical material describes IPEx as a 30 kg-class robotic excavator [3]. This is a mass class; no measured total mass for the flight-design IPEx was found in the sources reviewed. Mass determines launch, landing and mobility requirements, so this value must be confirmed from a primary source before any delivery assessment.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power requirements for IPEx were not publicly specified in the sources reviewed, and no power value is given here. Power architecture (for example, whether the robot draws from the lander or carries its own supply) is not described in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The target environment is the lunar south pole, where low sun angles produce long shadows and harsh lighting, and terrain can be featureless. NASA and the IPEx test-site authors both identify these lighting conditions as challenging for navigation and vision-based autonomy [1][4]. Dust is a central hazard for mechanisms, optics and thermal systems. The IPEx design addresses this with electrodynamic dust shields on its camera modules and a thermal control system with an actuated radiator cover [2]. Excavation must also fit the operating window available on the surface. NASA frames the IPEx goal as excavating up to 10,000 kg in a single lunar day [1]. Other general lunar conditions apply, including vacuum, large temperature variations and abrasive regolith, but no quantitative environmental qualification for IPEx was found in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: The payload class is described by general engineering goals rather than a flown or standardised design. IPEx has not been verified in flight or lunar operation. Autonomy has been evaluated in a terrestrial facility, and NASA states that autonomy testing is ongoing [1][4]. Excavation goals (such as 10,000 kg per lunar day) are targets, not measured performance [1]. Published mass, dimensions and power for the flight-design IPEx were not found in the sources reviewed. Test-facility results do not directly quantify performance in real lunar conditions [4].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: NASA's public IPEx page says only that IPEx will be 'sent to the Moon', with no date, mission or delivery plan given [1]. No lander, mission manifest or interface document for IPEx was verified. Any surface robotic experiment of this type would follow the surface-payload route described below, but the interface details are not established for IPEx.
transportation_process: Integrate the robot into a lander payload compartment or on a lander-supplied support structure on Earth. The interface is not verified for IPEx.
Launch the lander and robot on a launch vehicle.
Transfer towards the Moon and perform lunar orbit or descent operations.
Land the robot on the lunar surface with its stowage and release mechanism.
Release the robot, commission its systems, and check its navigation and excavation functions.
Connect or supply power, thermal management and communications, which must be defined for the specific mission.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The deployment mechanism for IPEx is not described in the sources reviewed. Robotic release from a lander is one possible method, but it is not verified for this design.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No flown autonomous excavation experiment is verified in the sources reviewed. The immediate lineage is the RASSOR excavator, which NASA describes as the TRL-4 precursor of IPEx [2].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Not assessed. No verified lander, rover or spacecraft interface data for IPEx or any other autonomous robotic experiment were found in the sources reviewed, so no lander compatibility is asserted.

article.historical_significance: Autonomous robotic excavation for ISRU is an emerging field. The sources reviewed show ground demonstration work rather than lunar operation. NASA documentation shows IPEx developing from the RASSOR excavator, which was at TRL 4, to the TRL 5 design described in 2024 [2]. Autonomy testing in a simulated south-pole facility was reported in 2025 [4]. The significance of this work is that it links early robotic excavation concepts to planned ISRU pilot plants. The ARISE project shows parallel interest in autonomous robot teams for lunar prospecting, although it describes a proposal and simulation [5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name describes a class of robotic ISRU experiments rather than one standard design, and no universal mass, power or performance figure applies to the class. The IPEx figures used here are either NASA goals (such as 10,000 kg of regolith per lunar day), laboratory scaling values (drum dimensions from ground tests), or facility dimensions. None is a measured lunar performance. Mass, dimensions and power for the flight-design IPEx are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. A dry-mass target of 30 kg was reported in a secondary summary of NASA technical material but was not verified in the primary paper reviewed, so it is not used as a specification in this article. The ARISE project page describes a proposal and simulation and does not report outcomes or lunar operation.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were added because no direct image asset URL was verified from an official page in this run; NASA IPEx page images were listed by the page but not verified.

data_quality_notes: No images are included. Image assets on the NASA IPEx page were listed but not opened or verified, so no image URL is asserted. Image research is outstanding.
The IPEx flight-design mass, dimensions and power are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The 30 kg-class description is a mass class from NASA technical material [3].
A dry-mass target of 30 kg against a 65 kg RASSOR 2.0 baseline was reported in a secondary search summary; it was not verified in a primary source and is not used as a specification.

The NASA IPEx PDF (NTRS 20240008162 download) could not be rendered for text extraction in this run. Its abstract and citation metadata were used instead. Design details from that paper are therefore limited to the abstract-level summary.
The NASA IPEx page refers to a 'Lunar Autonomy Challenge' using a digital twin of IPEx; this is not treated as hardware or mission evidence.
No IPEx flight manifest, launch date or lander interface was verified. Artemis schedule results from a search were not used because they did not mention IPEx.
The ARISE project period (01.03.2023 to 29.02.2024) is as stated on the project page; its funder, partners and outcomes are not stated there.
Lab bucket-drum dimensions are scaling-test values, not IPEx flight dimensions.
